t: Introduction to the topic: gunshot injuries
n: Introduction to the topic: gunshot injuries. Gunshot injuries are encountered in forensic practice less often than mechanical injuries inflicted by blunt and sharp objects. Nevertheless, law enforcement authorities pay special attention to such events and conduct a thorough investigation. The outline is as follows: the structure of weapons and cartridges, damaging factors, the range of fire, entrance and exit holes, and blast trauma. The aim of the class is to learn to draw conclusions about the weapon, the range and the direction of the wound track from the features of the injury.

t: The concept and particular character of a gunshot injury
n: The concept and particular character of a gunshot injury. With such a weapon, the damaging factor is set in motion by the energy of powder gases; the injury inflicted by it is called a gunshot injury. The projectile has a comparatively small mass but a high velocity; therefore the injury may be inflicted even from a great distance. Besides the mechanical factor, thermal, chemical and other kinds of action are observed. This particular character is connected with the structure of the weapon and ammunition, which is why a gunshot injury differs from injuries by blunt and sharp objects.

Two groups of injuries. In forensic medicine these injuries are conditionally divided into two groups. The first is the gunshot injury, in which a firearm and powder gases take part; this group is important in peacetime as well. The second is blast trauma, caused by a shell, mine, grenade and explosive substance. Injuries from the explosion of a shell, mine or grenade are observed mainly in combat conditions. In peacetime, injuries from firearms and explosions are significant for forensic examination.

Classification of firearms. By purpose, military, hunting, sporting, gas and special firearms are distinguished. A typical weapon is made in a factory under special conditions; an atypical weapon is home-made or altered, for example a rifle with a shortened barrel. Among firearms there are individual weapons: rifle, assault rifle, pistol; and a group weapon, the machine gun. Artillery weapons make up a separate group.

Barrel, rifling and calibre. By its inner surface, a barrel may be smooth-bore or rifled; a military barrel has 4–6 helical grooves. The grooves give the bullet a rotating motion, as a result of which the bullet flies faster, farther and more accurately. In a smooth-bore hunting barrel, the calibre is defined by the number of balls obtained from 1 pound, that is, 453.6 g of lead. By length, a long barrel is characteristic of a rifle and carbine, a medium barrel of a submachine gun, and a short barrel of a pistol and revolver. The rifled calibre is up to 6 mm, 7–9 mm, or 10 mm and larger.

t: Hunting, sporting, gas and special weapons
n: Hunting, sporting, gas and special weapons. Hunting weapons have a smooth-bore or rifled barrel. Smooth-bore hunting weapons are intended for firing shot and have from 1 to 4 barrels. The calibre of smooth-bore hunting weapons is from 10 to 32; 12 and 16 are more common. Some have both a smooth-bore and a rifled barrel and fire bullets and shot. Sporting weapons hardly differ in structure from military ones; the barrel is usually of small calibre, 5.6 mm, and rifled. Special firearms also use the energy of powder gases: starting, signal and construction-assembly pistols belong to this group.

The first quick question. Question: how are weapons grouped by purpose of manufacture and use? Answer: military, hunting, sporting, gas and special firearms. Question: how do weapons differ by barrel length? Answer: long, that is, rifle and carbine; medium, that is, submachine gun; short, that is, pistol and revolver. Question: what is the calibre of a rifled barrel? Answer: the distance between opposite lands of the rifling, in millimetres. Small up to 6 mm, medium 7–9 mm, large 10 mm and above. Attention: in a smooth-bore hunting weapon, the larger the calibre number, the smaller the diameter of the shot and of the barrel bore.

Structure of a military cartridge. In a unitary cartridge, the projectile, that is, the bullet, the powder charge and the primer are placed together as one in the case. Composition of the primer: lead styphnate as initiator, antimony as fuel, and Berthollet's salt as oxidiser. The tip of the bullet of a long-barrelled weapon is slightly pointed; in a short-barrelled weapon the tip is rounded or in the shape of a truncated cone. The firing chain proceeds in four stages. First the hammer strikes the primer. The primer ignites the powder. The powder gases create pressure. And finally the projectile leaves the barrel.

Powder and special bullets. Smokeless powder gives more powerful energy, so the bullet damages a distant target better. The basis of smokeless powder is nitrocellulose; when 1 g burns it gives 3 times more gas than black powder, and it is used in military and sporting weapons. Black powder consists of potassium nitrate, charcoal and sulphur; when 1 g burns it gives about 300 cubic cm of gas, and it is used in hunting weapons and signal pistols. The basis of an armour-piercing bullet is special steel; an incendiary one contains phosphorus, and a tracer barium and magnesium compounds. An explosive bullet breaks into small parts on the target; international agreements prohibit it in combat.

Structure of a shot cartridge. The case is made of brass, plastic or cardboard; the powder is closed with a felt, cardboard or plastic wad. The layers of the cartridge in order are as follows: case and primer, powder charge, cardboard or felt wad, shot, then the shot wad. Shot is pellets from 1 to 5.5 mm in diameter; larger ones are called buckshot. In a bullet cartridge for a smooth-bore weapon there is a spherical bullet more than 10 mm in diameter, a Zhakan or Brenneke bullet.

The first case analysis: weapon and cartridge. Situation: a rifle with a shortened barrel and butt was found at the scene. Such a weapon is not typical but atypical. The cartridge case is of cardboard, and inside are powder, wads and pellets 6 mm in diameter. This corresponds to the structure of a shot cartridge. Question: are the pellets shot or buckshot? In a hunting weapon with what kind of barrel is such a cartridge used: smooth-bore or rifled? Attention: risk of error. Shot, that is, 1–5.5 mm, is not buckshot; buckshot is a pellet larger than shot.

Damaging factors of a shot. The burning of powder in 0.01–0.001 s creates a large gas pressure and expels the projectile from the barrel. Kinds of action: mechanical, thermal, chemical and complex; most factors act mechanically. The action of additional factors depends on the structure of the weapon and cartridge, previous shots and obstacles. Groups of factors: the main projectile, that is, the bullet, shot and their parts. Additional factors: air ahead of the bullet, flame, gases, soot and powder. Factors of the firearm: recoil and bursting of the barrel. Secondary projectile: the obstacle, clothing and bone fragments.

t: Pressure of powder gases and projectile velocity
n: Pressure of powder gases and projectile velocity. The powder burns in 0.01–0.001 s, creates gas pressure and expels the projectile from the barrel. The pressure also acts on all sides of the barrel wall, which is why the weapon moves slightly backward. Especially in a home-made weapon the barrel may burst and injure the person holding the weapon. Figures: in a smooth-bore barrel the pressure is 400–700 atm and the projectile velocity up to 500 m/s. In a rifled barrel the pressure is 2000–3000 atm. In the Makarov pistol the projectile velocity is 315 m/s, in the AKM assault rifle 710 m/s.

Mechanical action: bursting, punching and wedging. In 1849 Pirogov described a tissue defect, that is, minus-tissue, calling it "loss of tissue substance". In bursting action the energy is several thousand joules, the wound is several times larger than the projectile, and the edges are uneven. In punching action the energy is several hundred joules, the defect is small, and the edges are even. In wedging action the energy is several tens of joules, the wound is slit-like or stellate, and there is no tissue defect. Bursting action may also occur in contact shots, and with special bullets and bullets with a displaced centre of gravity. Air ahead of the bullet acts mechanically at a distance of 3–5 cm, and powder gases at 10–15 cm.

Thermal and chemical action. The muzzle flame is formed by the explosion of incompletely burnt powder particles with atmospheric oxygen and acts at a distance of 3–10 cm. Flame and powder gases scorch clothing, skin and hair; secondary ignition of clothing also causes thermal injury. Around the entrance hole, carboxyhaemoglobin forms in the blood and carboxymyoglobin in the muscle, and the area takes on a pink hue. Special bullets containing an incendiary or chemical substance cause thermal and chemical injury respectively.

The second case analysis: damaging factors. Situation: around the entrance hole there are soot, powder and metal particles. There are no signs of burning or of the action of powder gases. Question: to which zone of close range does this correspond, and which additional factors acted? Answer: the second zone. There is no sign of powder gases, and the hole is formed only by the action of the bullet; for most military weapons this is 25–35 cm. Attention: a pink hue and burning are characteristic of powder gases. Soot, powder and metal particles act only superficially and weakly.

Range and distance of fire. Attention: range is not distance. The range is a set of features, whereas the distance is the length from the muzzle to the target. The same range may correspond to different distances in units of length in weapons of different makes. The range is determined from the features; for the distance, an experiment is carried out with the same weapon and cartridge. There are three kinds of range: contact fire, in which the muzzle is in contact with the target; close range, in which there are signs of additional factors and three zones are distinguished; and non-close range, in which there are no signs of additional factors.

Injury in contact fire. In full contact, the muzzle touches with its whole surface; soot and powder are found inside the wound track. If powder gases reach a cavity, rupture of internal organs is possible; at the start of the track the tissue is pink. In hermetic contact, an abrasion or bruise corresponding to the section of the muzzle forms on the skin; it is called a muzzle imprint. Kinds: in fully hermetic position, a muzzle imprint corresponding to the muzzle remains on the skin. In full contact the defect is larger than the calibre, with ragged edges. In oblique contact there is a tear on one side and tongue-shaped soot.

The second quick question. Question 1: are range and distance the same? No. Range is a set of features, that is, contact, close, non-close; distance is the interval between the muzzle and the target. Question 2: how is the distance of fire determined? From the same weapon and the same cartridges, shots are fired at a similar object from different distances and the injuries are compared. Question 3: what mark remains on the skin in fully hermetic contact fire? An imprint in the form of an abrasion or bruise corresponding to the section of the muzzle, that is, a "muzzle imprint". Attention: in contact fire, soot and powder are found in the wound track, and at the start of the track the tissue is pink, owing to carboxyhaemoglobin and carboxymyoglobin.

Close range: three zones. The length of a zone depends on the length of the barrel, the calibre and the structure of the cartridge. In zones 1–2, as the distance increases, the area covered becomes larger; in zone 3 the number of particles decreases. If there is an obstacle, the additional factors remain on the obstacle; the bullet is deformed, and an atypical injury may form. In zone 1 there are powder gas, soot, particles and oil; the distance is ≈1 cm for the Makarov, ≤3 cm for the Kalashnikov, ≈5 cm for a rifle. In zone 2 there is no powder gas, but there are soot, particles and oil; for most military weapons 25–35 cm. In zone 3 there are only powder and metal particles; 150 cm for the Makarov, 200 for the Kalashnikov, 250 for a rifle.

t: Non-close range and the Vinogradov phenomenon
n: Non-close range and the Vinogradov phenomenon. At non-close range, no signs of additional factors are detected around the entrance hole. Conditions of the phenomenon: velocity not less than 500 m/s, clothing not closely fitting the body, no strong wind. The mechanism has five stages. First, the bullet velocity is not less than 500 m/s. Second, a low-pressure space appears behind the bullet. Third, soot enters this space. Fourth, the bullet passes through the first obstacle. Fifth, the soot remains on the inner surface. Attention: unlike close range, there is no soot on the outer surface of the 1st layer of clothing; the amount of soot is small.

The third case analysis: determining the range. Situation: around the injury there is no soot on the outer surface of the first layer of clothing, while on the inner surface of the clothing there is a small amount of soot. Which range? This may be the Vinogradov phenomenon. Conditions: bullet velocity not less than 500 m/s, clothing not closely fitting the body, no strong wind. Attention: in close range, soot is also present on the outer surface of the first layer of clothing; in the Vinogradov phenomenon it is not. In the phenomenon the soot is scanty and its intensity increases towards the periphery. In close range the opposite is observed.

t: Morphology: the theory of shock action
n: Morphology: the theory of shock action. The morphology of an injury depends on three groups of factors: the projectile, its ballistics, and the characteristics of the injured region. The theory of shock action: the projectile delivers a strong blow to a small area, and the force spreads sideways and backward as well. The pulsation of the temporary cavity creates phases of positive and negative pressure and favours deeper penetration of the bullet. Zones in the wound wall: the wound track itself; the contusion zone 0.3–2 cm; the concussion zone 4–5 cm and more.

t: Types of wound and the wound track
n: Types of wound and the wound track. Attention: a blind wound is not a tangential wound. In a perforating wound there are an entrance, a track and an exit; in a blind one there is no exit and the bullet remains at the end of the track; in a tangential one the bullet does not enter the body completely. In a tangential injury, an elongated abrasion or a wound with a groove-like depression in the middle part is formed. The track may be straight, broken or arc-shaped. An interrupted track is formed by contraction of certain tissues and usually indicates that the injury was vital. A bullet with a displaced centre of gravity loses stability: a large track, rupture of an internal organ, bone fracture. In a thin region there may be two entrances and two exits.

t: Entrance hole: rims and tissue defect
n: Entrance hole: rims and tissue defect. As the bullet enters, its side rubs against the skin and forms an abrasion rim 1–3 mm wide at the edges of the entrance hole. The outer diameter of the rim is equal to the diameter of the projectile; in soft regions, that is, the abdomen and buttock, it is wider than near bones. Particles of soot and oil on the surface of the bullet form a contamination rim at the edge of the wound; the two rims overlap. If the edges of a wound with a tissue defect are brought together, folds of skin form around it; if there is no defect, the edges coincide. This test was described by Pirogov in 1865.

t: Bullet mark on bones: flat and tubular bone
n: Bullet mark on bones: flat and tubular bone. In a flat bone, at the point where the bullet entered, a defect in the form of a truncated cone is formed; the direction of the projectile is from the small base to the large base. In a long tubular bone, on the side where the bullet entered, a round defect with radial cracks is found. On the side where the bullet exited, the bone defect is larger, and the cracks starting from it run longitudinally. If near the exit hole the body was pressed against a hard object, an abrasion rim may form at the edge.

t: Difference between entrance and exit holes
n: The difference between entrance and exit holes. In close range, signs of additional factors are present only around the entrance hole and not at the exit. At the entrance, a cuff-like haemorrhage in the soft tissue; at the exit, an asymmetric haemorrhage. Shape: the entrance is round or oval, the exit slit-like, arc-shaped or stellate. The wound edges at the entrance are relatively even and inverted; at the exit uneven and everted. A tissue defect is often present at the entrance, rarely at the exit. At the entrance there are abrasion, 1–3 mm, and contamination rims; at the exit they are more often absent. Attention: the apex of the defect cone points inward at the entrance, and, when present, outward at the exit.

The third quick question. Question: in which hole are the abrasion and contamination rims distinct? Answer: in the entrance hole; at the exit they are often absent. Question: how does a blind injury differ from a perforating one? Answer: there is no exit hole; the projectile remains at the end of the wound track. Question: what is the defect in a flat bone at the site of bullet entry? Answer: a truncated cone; the bullet direction is from the small base to the large base. Question: how does the exit side differ in a tubular bone? Answer: the defect is larger and the cracks longitudinal; on the entrance side there are radial cracks.

t: Case analysis 4: entrance and exit holes
n: The fourth case analysis: entrance and exit holes. Situation: on a body, hole A is round, with even edges inverted; around it a rim of abrasion and contamination 1–3 mm wide. Hole B is slit-like, with uneven edges everted; there are no rims, and the haemorrhages are asymmetrically placed. In a flat bone, on the side of A, a defect in the form of a truncated cone. In a tubular bone, on one side a round defect and radial cracks, on the other a large defect. Question: which hole is the entrance and which the exit? What do the defects in the bones show about the direction of the wound track?

Injury from a shot cartridge. A shot cartridge is used in smooth-bore hunting guns. Close range is longer with these weapons. Signs of powder and metal particles can be detected at 200–500 cm. Shot flies 200–400 m, buckshot up to 600 m; the wad acts up to 40 m. The wounds are usually blind. Dependence on distance: in contact or up to 1 m the action is compact, there is one entrance hole and it equals the diameter of the cartridge. Up to 5 m there is relative scatter, a main hole and small wounds around it. Beyond 5 m there is scatter, and small, similar wounds are formed.

Blank, gas and pneumatic weapons. A blank cartridge has no projectile: the injury in contact or close-range fire is formed by powder gases. Here powder gases and the wad act, and in contact fire a blind wound and rupture of internal organs are possible. A gas weapon temporarily incapacitates a person; the irritant effect lasts about an hour, with consequences up to 7 days. Lacrimation and cough are observed, with action at 2–3 m. In a pneumatic weapon the projectile flies by compressed air, up to 30–50 m; it does not penetrate the body, there are no traces of additional factors, and the wound is blind.

t: Forensic examination questions in gunshot injuries
n: Forensic examination questions in gunshot injuries. The questions: was the injury inflicted by a firearm, what weapon and projectile, the range and distance, entrance and exit holes, the direction of the wound track. It is also determined: the mutual position of the barrel and the victim, the sequence of injuries, whether the weapon is automatic, and whether the victim inflicted the injury himself. That the injury is from a firearm is shown by the tissue defect, abrasion and contamination rims, traces of additional factors and finding the projectile in the body. The range is determined from a set of features; the distance, however, is determined only by experiment with that weapon and cartridge. Determining the kind of weapon is more difficult.

t: Sequence, self-inflicted shot and methods of examination
n: Sequence, self-inflicted shot and methods of examination. In the first injury the haemorrhage is more marked. With an automatic weapon, many injuries are on one side and are similar. In a self-inflicted shot there is soot on the surface of the hand, the nose and the ear; traces of blood may be found on the muzzle and the palm. The physician must record the entrance and exit holes and the wound track, and hand over the bullet and clothing to the law enforcement authorities. Instrumental methods: radiography detects bullets and shot in the body. Soft X-rays find metal particles around the entrance. Ultraviolet light shows small amounts of soot and oil. Infrared photography detects soot, powder and metal on dark clothing.

Explosion: kinds, burning and detonation. The release of a large amount of energy in a very short time on a physical or chemical change of substances is called an explosion. Kinds of explosion according to Strehlow and Bacer, 1976: natural, that is, lightning, volcano, meteorite; deliberate; accidental, that is, gas cylinders and steam boilers. Burning is comparatively slow; the burning rate of black powder in a closed medium reaches 400 m/s and yields gas at a pressure of several thousand atmospheres. In detonation the transformation occurs under the action of a shock wave, at a velocity of several thousand m/s; in TNT the pressure is more than 100,000 atm.

Classification of explosives. By state of aggregation, explosives are solid, liquid and gaseous. Primary, that is, initiating, substances are very sensitive to impact: they are used in primers and detonators; for example mercury cyanide, lead trinitroresorcinate. Secondary, that is, high-explosive (brisant), substances are initiated by detonation; they are used in shells, grenades, mines, bombs, construction and mining: TNT, ammonal. Propellants do not detonate but decompose by burning: powder. Pyrotechnic compositions are mixtures of oxidiser and fuel, used in signal and illuminating rockets.

t: Kinds of action of explosive factors
n: Kinds of action of explosive factors. Explosion gases show mechanical action, that is, bursting, contused wounds and bruises; thermal action, that is, burns of skin and hair; and chemical action, that is, the action of carboxyhaemoglobin. The shock wave of the surrounding medium acts like a blunt object with an unlimited flat surface: injury occurs on the surface facing the centre of the explosion. The initial velocity of fragments of the device is up to several thousand m/s; abrasions, wounds, bone fractures, injury to internal organs and separation of body parts are possible. Baro-acoustic trauma is mainly from the shock wave: the eardrum and the lungs are damaged. Injuries from secondary projectiles are usually milder.

t: Blast trauma: kinds and damaging factors
n: Blast trauma: kinds and damaging factors. An explosion is the release of a large amount of energy in a very short time. Kinds: natural, deliberate and accidental. Substances: primary, for example mercury cyanide, and secondary, for example TNT, detonate; propellants, that is, powder, burn. Kinds of action: mechanical, thermal, chemical and baro-acoustic; in the last the eardrum and lungs are damaged. An explosion has five damaging factors: detonation products, that is, explosion gases and particles; the shock wave of the surrounding medium; fragments of the explosive device; special means; and secondary projectiles, that is, fragments of clothing, footwear and objects.

Ranges of explosion. The distance corresponding to each range depends on the explosive, the device and the power of the charge. In the explosion of a device without a charge, the kind of injury depends on the intermediate distance and surrounding objects. In a cylinder, wall fragments; in a steam boiler, thermal; with gas, coal, flour dust, thermal injury and injury from the shock wave. Four ranges are distinguished. At contact range, the main factors are the products and fragments of the device. At close range, the products, fragments and shock wave. At relatively close range, the shock wave, fragments and projectiles. At non-close range, the fragments and secondary projectiles.

The fifth case analysis: an explosion situation. Situation: after an explosion, fragments of the device were found in the victim's clothing and body. On the surface of the body facing the explosion there are mechanical injuries. Question 1: which of the four ranges of an explosion, that is, contact, close, relatively close and non-close, may correspond to this situation? Attention: the exact distance corresponding to a range depends on the power of the charge and the characteristics of the device. Injury to the eardrum and lungs is also assessed. Question 2: how does the physician document the injuries? To whom and within what period are foreign bodies found on the clothing and body handed over?

Conclusion and control questions. A gunshot injury is inflicted by a projectile set in motion by the energy of powder gases. Injuries from explosions are also included in this group. Attention: range is not distance. Range is a set of features, that is, contact, close, non-close; distance is the interval between the muzzle and the target and is determined by experiment. The entrance hole is even, inverted, with abrasion and contamination rims. The exit hole is uneven, everted, without rims. Review: how a gunshot injury differs from other injuries, the classification of weapons, the structure of the cartridge, damaging factors and the kinds of their action.
